# On the Strange Comfort of Uncertainty

I've been thinking about how we've become obsessed with certainty, and how that obsession might be ruining us in ways we don't quite acknowledge.

There's a particular moment in the early morning, that liminal space between sleep and waking, where I find myself suspended in uncertainty about what day it is, what I need to do, whether I'm late for something. Most people probably hate that feeling—there's a reason we reach for our phones immediately, why we want to anchor ourselves in the solid ground of facts and schedules. But I've started to treasure those few seconds of beautiful not-knowing.

We live in an age of unprecedented access to information. I can look up almost anything within seconds. I can check the weather, read breaking news, see what my friends had for lunch three thousand miles away, find the answer to any question that pops into my head. And yet—and I think this is the thing nobody talks about enough—this has somehow made us more anxious, not less. We've traded the comfort of mystery for the tyranny of total transparency, and I'm not sure it was a good deal.

When I was younger, before smartphones became ubiquitous, there was a different texture to uncertainty. If you didn't know something, you just... didn't know it. You could wonder about it, speculate, imagine multiple possibilities without needing to resolve the question immediately. There was space for ambiguity in daily life. You could be uncertain about whether someone was angry with you—you might not find out until you saw them next. That uncertainty could be uncomfortable, sure, but it also created a kind of mental freedom. You couldn't constantly confirm or deny your worries.

Now, we can know almost everything about everyone almost immediately. A text left on read becomes a crisis to be analyzed. We can track our steps, our sleep, our heart rate, our productivity. We can see exactly how many people liked our posts and in what order. We've instrumentalized knowledge, turned it into a tool for managing not just the external world but our internal emotional landscape. And the paradox is that it hasn't made life feel more manageable—it's made it feel like we're constantly failing some invisible test.

I wonder sometimes if the drive for certainty isn't itself a kind of anxiety disorder that's become culturally normalized. We need to know outcomes before we experience them. We need to know what everyone thinks of us. We need to plan our entire futures with precision. We've lost the capacity to simply show up to something without knowing exactly what will happen, and I think that's a loss.

There's a wonderful concept in Japanese aesthetics called "ma"—the space between things, the silence between notes in music, the emptiness that gives shape to form. The idea is that what's not there is just as important as what is. Uncertainty is the ma of life. It's the space where possibility lives. And we're frantically trying to fill it in, to replace every unknown with data, every mystery with explanation.

I've noticed that the people I know who seem most at peace are the ones who've somehow made peace with not knowing. Not in a passive, give-up-on-life way, but in an active way—they've decided to tolerate uncertainty because they've recognized that certainty is actually impossible. The future will always surprise us. Other people's feelings will always be somewhat opaque. Our own motivations will always contain contradictions. And rather than fighting that, they've learned to move through it.

One of my favorite books is full of stories about people doing things without being able to predict the outcome. A woman leaves her job without another one lined up. Someone falls in love with a complete stranger. A person decides to move across the world on a whim. These things terrify me when I read them, and that's exactly why they fascinate me. There's something brave about choosing to act without perfect information.

The truth is, most of the best things in my life have come from uncertainty. I wouldn't have met some of my closest friends if I hadn't shown up to events not knowing anyone. I wouldn't have my job if I hadn't applied for something I wasn't entirely sure I could do. I wouldn't have learned anything if I'd stuck only to what I already knew I was competent at.

But we're being trained, increasingly, to optimize our lives, to minimize risk, to gather all available data before making decisions. We're told this is rational, this is smart. And sometimes it is. But sometimes it's just fear dressed up in the language of prudence.

I think about how people used to fall in love without swiping through hundreds of potential partners, how they'd move to new cities on a hope and a prayer, how they'd choose careers based on passion rather than salary potential and job market trends. I'm not romanticizing the past—those times had their own complications, their own forms of suffering. But there was a different relationship to uncertainty then, one that might have included more possibility.

What strikes me now is how much of my anxiety doesn't come from actual problems but from the need to resolve uncertainty prematurely. I can spend hours worrying about something that might never happen, trying to preemptively arrange my mental furniture for every possible outcome. But I could also just... wait. See what happens. Trust myself to handle it when it comes, if it comes.

There's a freedom in that, I think. Not in denying reality or refusing to plan, but in accepting that some things simply cannot be known in advance. And that's okay. That's actually just what being alive is.

So I'm trying, in small ways, to sit with uncertainty more. To not immediately Google every passing thought. To let a question remain unanswered for a while. To surprise myself. To remember that not knowing what's coming next isn't a failure of preparation—it's the basic condition of existence, and somehow, people have managed to live through it for thousands of years.

Maybe that morning feeling of not-knowing isn't something to fear or fix. Maybe it's a gift—a reminder that the future is still open, that anything could happen, that I'm not locked into a predetermined path. 

Maybe the discomfort of uncertainty is actually just the feeling of possibility.
